years of governance in the not-for-profit NGO sector, as well as an

Kia ora, and thank you for this opportunity.
My name is Anne-Marie Sutcliffe. I'm a registered psychiatric nurse
and general manager of community services for Lifewise and
Methodist Mission Northern. I've got a 40-year history of working in
mental health and community services, as well as working in the public service
sector.
My
services at Lifewise and Methodist Mission Northern sit across a really
broad and connected system for people and whanau, and those
people and whanau are among some of the most vulnerable in our community.
I've got services that work in housing and homelessness responses
and homelessness outreach and family and community services,
early childhood education, and wellbeing support.
We aim to support people with practical pathways back into
connection, safety, and stability.
And together, all of those services work as one system.
We go and we meet people where they are, we build trusted relationships over
time, and we try and link people to the right support so that their immediate
need, their long-term wellbeing, and wider community safety are addressed
together.
Yeah. So we don't intend to repeat the submission.
You've got that. But essentially, we do want to urge the Select
Committee not to support the Summary Offences
Amendment Bill because in our view, it does criminalize rough
sleeping and begging without addressing the root
causes of homelessness, addiction, trauma,
poverty, or mental health need.
In our experience, safer communities are created when
people are supported into safe accommodation with
effective wraparound services, not when they're
displaced from public spaces or pushed into less
visible and less safe places.
Existing legal powers already allow police, council,
and business owners to respond to genuine harm,
including breach of the peace, trespass, obstruction, disorderly
behavior, and breaches of local bylaws.
This bill, in our view, risks undermining years of
trust-based, trauma-informed work between
outreach teams, street whanau, businesses, police, council,
and other community services, while increasing the pressure on the
justice system and public services rather than
delivering better outcomes at a lower cost.
If the bill proceeds, Lifewise strongly recommends that rough
sleeping, intent to inhabit, and begging are
removed as grounds for a move on order, and that police must
first connect people with an accredited social service provider
with additional safeguards for young people under 17 through whanau,
legal guardians, or Oranga Tamariki.
So I want to just talk really briefly about a story from our outreach team, and
this is really talking to the people aspects.
This story's not unusual actually.
It's painfully common. We met a person because they kept
coming back to Merge, our community services cafe on Karanga-a-Hape
Road. That person was sleeping rough.
They'd already been told to move on many, many times.
More times than they can count, actually. They weren't asking for much from us.
They wanted a coffee. They wanted somewhere warm.
They wanted somewhere predictable, and somewhere where they could be seen without
being judged.
But over time with this person, as we got to know them, we learned that being
moved on, to them, didn't feel neutral.
It felt absolutely frightening. They'd lived through trauma in their
past life, and being approached by authority, being told to
leave suddenly, and being treated as a problem when they were
simply trying to survive sent them into a panic.
So they moved, but they didn't move into housing.
They moved into darker, more isolated places.
And it took weeks of consistent contact with us before they trusted
us enough after that experience to talk about getting some support.
And finally that happened, not because we pressured them or threatened them or
demanded compliance, but because we stayed with them.
Same people, time and time again, and we built a relationship,
and they knew that we would still be there tomorrow.
And for us, this is what move on orders risk breaking.
When people are forced to leave familiar places, they don't just disappear.
They become harder to find, harder to help, more
isolated, more afraid, and more at risk.
And importantly, trust gets reset to zero.
So what eventually helped this person wasn't enforcement, it
was relationship, dignity, being known by name, being met
with patience instead of punishment.
And that's why this proposed law worries us, both from a systemic
approach, but also from an operational on the streets approach.
Every day we see safer communities are built by connection,
not by exclusion, by housing people, supporting people,
and staying with people long enough for trust to grow.
For me, the key messages are clear.
Move on orders don't solve homelessness.
Housing and support solves homelessness, and trust is
what makes that change possible.
So what we're asking the committee to be clear about is
what is this bill trying to solve? What's the problem
definition that we're trying to resolve?
And then to be equally clear about what it will actually
do. If a person is rough sleeping, has set up their
belongings, or is sitting quietly with a sign asking for help,
they're not creating homelessness.
They're showing us where homelessness already exists.
Moving them on does not create a home, it doesn't create a health
response, doesn't create an income or a safe place to sleep.
It simply pushes people further from the relationships and
services that can help, and it risks turning poverty,
trauma, and survival into matters for police and the courts.
So our call to action is straightforward.
Do not support this bill in its current form.
At a minimum, remove rough sleeping, intent to inhabit, and begging
as grounds for a move on order.
Require police to connect people with accredited social services
before any enforcement steps are taken, and require stronger
safeguards in place for young people.
The committee has a choice here to endorse a response that
displaces people, or to strengthen one that connects
people to safety, dignity, and support.
We urge you to choose the second path.
Just in closing,
as we mark Matariki, a time for reflection, renewal,
and dreaming of what is possible, Lifewise exhorts the
government and all political parties to work towards a more just
future for everyone in Aotearoa, New Zealand.
That future must be shaped by systems, policies, and public
services that uphold dignity, strengthen
belonging, and create a genuinely human experience for all
people, especially those that are most vulnerable and too
often pushed to the margins. A just society for all
is what we ask for.
We're very happy to answer any questions you might have.
Thanks, Pam. Thank you Anne Marie. Really appreciate it.

There's lots of different ways that you can engage with somebody who's terrified

bylaw, but also builds trust. So you can be pushed
awake by a foot, or you can be woken by somebody who
crouches down and speaks to you gently.
Yeah. And that's obviously the second approach is what we would--
and the bylaws give the possibility of doing that.
There's nothing against that in the bylaws.
Thank you, and Dan Rosewarne.

impact would that have on your ability to connect people with
housing, healthcare, addiction support, and those other
services?
Yeah. Me?
Yeah.
So our experience is we work in the central Auckland
area, along with Ka Hutia Kaha and Auckland City Mission.
We know where people are, we know who people are, and
we don't double up services. We're very careful about that, but
we know where to go to engage with people.
When people are moved along,
they're going to move out and out and out, and

It's a frightening experience to be moved on by the police for

Thank you.

Thank you.

I worked in social services for over 30 years,
including as a mental health support worker and as a social worker.
And I'm also a climate activist, and I see
links between the social justice issues that are raised by this bill,
the effects of colonization, and the climate and ecological
emergency.
I'm opposed to this Summary Offences Bill.
I see it as an attempt to conceal the consequences
of the failure of our society to provide the basic necessities of
life for everyone.
And that failure is just one symptom of the failure of our
economic system,
which has not only failed to deliver homes for all our citizens,
it's failed to honor Crown obligations to Māori,
failed to reduce the emissions that are leading to catastrophic climate
change, and it's failed to protect our environments from
biodiversity loss and ecological breakdown.
But anyway, to return to the bill,
my concerns include the vulnerability of youth,
disregard for the principles of totality, and the callous
attitude towards some of the least fortunate members of our
society.
The evidence from the University of Otago reports that nearly half
of all homeless people in Aotearoa are aged under
25. Most are homeless due to circumstances
outside of their control, such as family violence,
poverty, and overcrowding.
And youth may not comply with move on orders simply because there
is nowhere safe for them to go. Youth that have aged out of
Oranga Tamariki care, two-thirds of whom are Māori,
may have no whanau support, and the services for homeless
youth are extremely limited.
The Waitangi Tribunal in 2023 found that the
Crown had breached the principles of equity and active
protection in its lack of support for homeless rangatahi,
and this bill compounds that breach.
Research has consistently also shown that contact with the justice
system in adolescence leads to more frequent contact
later in life. So this bill increases the long-term risk for
homeless youth.
Criminalizing people who are in public places for safety reasons
or who are unable to comply with police due to mental distress
or cognitive issues when there are simply not enough resources
in the community to support them, it's unfair and it's
wrong.
The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists, the
Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission, and the Mental Health Foundation have
all highlighted in recent years increasing levels of mental
distress, particularly amongst young people,
and that the mental health services in Aotearoa are not
meeting those needs.
Nothing has substantially changed since
2023, when a report from 500 mental health
physicians concluded that the mental health
services in Aotearoa are not fit for purpose.
So yeah, this is something I've witnessed at first hand, the lack of
resources and the difficulty finding affordable and
supported accommodation for people with mental illness or with learning
disabilities. Workers in mental health do everything they can,
but there's no substitute for comprehensive and
properly resourced services. That's what we need.
Our services are fragmented.
They are siloed due to moves to tighten eligibility
criteria and funding over the years.
No one has the responsibility to follow through with an individual
and ensure that that person's needs are met.
Radio New Zealand reported just the other day that each month for the
past 16 months, there were 1,000 more
inquiries to MSD about emergency
housing than there were actual formal
applications submitted.
That's 1,000 people out there needing help
who didn't even get through to applying for it.
And for those who did make it to a formal application and were
declined, a third were offered nothing.
Nothing at all.
And these are issues well known to frontline workers like police.
Giving police powers to ask people to move on is just shifting the problem from
one place to another. We have citizens of Aotearoa
homeless and unwell in our streets.
About a third of homeless people are Maori, tangata whenua of
this land, suffering from the long-term effects of colonization,
loss of land, livelihood, and community, and we are just telling them to
go away. Brunis Hickey reported
that this government is currently building more prison beds than
beds in affordable homes.
That's a disgrace. It brings shame to this government and anyone who
supports this heartless legislation.
We know that there are not enough affordable homes in Aotearoa.
It's the result of housing being used for many years as an investment
and new kainga ora projects being stopped.
Over 3,000 planned new builds were stopped by this government.
Public housing is not an optional extra for society.
It's an essential service to provide all our citizens a
life of dignity.
Research evidence in Aotearoa shows unequivocally that the
answer to homelessness is support into suitable housing.
Well, who knew? Aotearoa is a rich
country, and the rich are becoming more and more wealthy.
The collective wealth of the country's 150 richest
individuals and families has grown, this is
mind-boggling, by $26.9 billion
in one year.
This is obscene when people are homeless and begging on the streets.
Poverty is increasing. The New Zealand Council of Christian
Social Services has shown that there are
473,000 people in Aotearoa
right now experiencing material hardship.
Poverty is the result of deliberate policies that have increased the gap between
rich and poor, such as maintaining levels of unemployment as a
strategy to reduce inflation, encouraging the use of housing as an
investment, and allowing virtual monopolies on food
supplies, privatizing services, user pays.
The list goes on. And now this government wants to hide the
results by moving people who demonstrate the
failure of their policies out of sight so we don't have to
look at the human cost.
What is the economy for if it is not to provide for the people of
Aotearoa, to provide the necessities of life, shelter
being the very first? An economy that fails to do that is a
failure, no matter what the books say.
So we see the parallel consequences resulting from government
policies focusing on a narrow view of economy
and growth. We see increased poverty and social injustice
alongside increasing wealth and the influence of an elite few.
We have blatant breaches of good faith surrounding Te Tiriti o
Waitangi alongside claims of equality in society,
and we have increasing climate-related emergencies and
threatened extinctions of our endemic wildlife alongside a
disregard for emissions reduction, plans to enable more
extractive industries, and treatment of the environment as a
disposable resource.
We're in the midst of a polycrisis that's not only a social
crisis like the one of homelessness and poverty, but an
environmental one of rising temperatures and unstable weather
events, and an international political crisis of
wars, resource scarcity, and displaced people.
Aotearoa cannot separate itself from the rest of the world in this and can't
deny that our social problems and our environmental problems are
linked by our political attitude.
The same short-term policies of exploitation and
prioritization of financial gain have resulted in the social
injustices we see in colonization, homelessness, and
the climate and ecological emergency we are all facing.
This legislation is in the same spirit as climate denial,
and I'm asking you now, reject this bill in its
entirety. Thank you.

demonstrated that providing emergency accommodation significantly reduced

Housing people costs money. Imprisoning them costs considerably

I believe New Zealand can do better than moving vulnerable people from place to
place. We should be investing in solutions that help people regain stability
rather than criminalizing them for being homeless.

bill to rough sleeping and begging is the

If this bill does continue unamended, it will paint an incredibly sad

don't know where that's gone.
That's all I have to say to the committee. I'm happy to take any questions.

the proposals that are being brought about by this government at the moment,

Camilla.

this bill applies to 14-year-olds.
